transcript:
Header: 2025-07-02 10:00 PDT | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Lydia Park (Quantaco Head of ML), Tom Reyes (Infra), Anika Bose (Product)

Summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect): Quick cost/unit economics review for POC; discussed tokens/sec/$, cache hit assumptions, batching tradeoffs and next steps for benchmarks and security docs.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Maya): All right good morning everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — cost review, results from last week's tuning, batching experiments, and next steps for the dedicated benchmark.
00:22 Speaker 2 (Lydia): Morning. We have about 30 minutes to go over costs; Tom is here for infra constraints, Anika is on product to confirm SLOs.
00:31 Speaker 1 (Maya): Great. Samir, do you want to kick off with the tokens per second per dollar slide?
00:38 Speaker 3 (Samir): Yeah sure. So, high level — we re-ran the microbenchmarks with the quantized 4-bit profile and with prefix caching turned on at 60% hit-rate assumption. The headline numbers: hosted baseline (single-tenant shared) we estimate ~12k tokens / $1 for generation workloads at p50 latency 120ms. With dedicated and optimized batching we get to about 28k tokens / $1 on the 4xA100 equivalent pool.
01:10 Speaker 4 (Tom): Wait, that delta is big — is that because of batching or the cost model (spot vs reserved)?
01:18 Speaker 3 (Samir): It's both. Dedicated drops the per-instance overhead, and our continuous batching engine improves tokens/sec when request sizes are small but frequent. Also quantization gains matter a fair amount — approx 1.6x throughput uplift on the LLM model we onboarded.
01:31 Speaker 2 (Lydia): About the caching assumption — we currently see a lot of shared prefixes in our FAQ traffic. Is 60% hit realistic? We saw 40% last week in the short trace.
01:43 Speaker 3 (Samir): Good question. The 60% was an optimistic mid-point — if you give us a 24h sample we can replay and give you a realistic cache-hit sensitivity curve. The tokens/sec/$ moves non-linearly with hit rate, since cache hits bypass attention recompute and avoid KV growth.
02:05 Speaker 1 (Maya): Can you give an example of the sensitivity?
02:08 Speaker 3 (Samir): Sure. Rough numbers from the model: at 40% hit we saw about 18k tokens/$, at 60% hit ~24-28k tokens/$ depending on request length distribution, and at 80% hit it asymptotes around 34k tokens/$. So caching is huge for the unit economics.
02:30 Speaker 5 (Anika): For product SLOs we need p95 < 300ms for chat flows under 100 tokens response. How do batching and cache interact with that?
02:39 Speaker 3 (Samir): There's a tradeoff. Aggressive batching increases tokens/sec but can harm latency tail. Our runtime supports latency-aware batching — you can set a max batching latency (e.g., 15ms) and then there's also dynamic batching that backs off for low concurrency. In the tests we ran with max batch latency 20ms, p95 was 270ms and throughput was 1.8x better than without batching.
03:05 Speaker 4 (Tom): And how does that compare on Dedicated vs Hosted? We want consistent p95 across both; we can't have the hosted service occasionally spike.
03:13 Speaker 3 (Samir): Dedicated gives more predictable throughput since you control the pool and scheduling; hosted has slightly higher variance but we do SLA tiers. For your scale and SLA needs I'd recommend Dedicated for production after the POC.
03:26 Speaker 2 (Lydia): For cost modeling, can you share the raw tokens/sec numbers per GPU configuration? The spreadsheet had aggregated tokens/$ but we want per-GPU metrics to plug into our cost planning.
03:36 Speaker 1 (Maya): Samir shared a draft sheet last week, Samir will update with per-GPU rows.
03:42 Speaker 3 (Samir): Yep. Example: 1xA100 equiv (quantized) — ~7k tokens/sec sustained; 2x equiv pooled ~13k, 4x equiv ~30k with batching at 16. These are synthetic steady-state numbers. Your real-world will be shaped by request length and repeat prefixes.
04:05 Speaker 5 (Anika): On prefixes — do you do prefix coalescing across users or is it per-customer? Any privacy concerns?
04:14 Speaker 3 (Samir): It's per-customer within your dedicated pool unless you choose cross-tenant caching in hosted setups (we don't do cross-customer caching in shared mode). For private/on-prem we leave cache control to you. All cached KV entries are encrypted at rest with customer KMS keys in Dedicated/Private.
04:35 Speaker 4 (Tom): Good. We also asked about token accounting for system prompts and tool calls — are those in the tokens/sec metrics?
04:43 Speaker 3 (Samir): Yes all tokens that traverse inference are accounted. For tool/call overhead it's usually small but when you have many short tool calls it can add up. We recommend batching tool calls where possible.
04:55 Speaker 1 (Maya): Let's walk through the benchmark results you ran last week, Samir — the one with batch sizes 1/8/16 and caching on/off.
05:03 Speaker 3 (Samir): Sure. I uploaded the logs to the shared folder; quick summary: without caching and batch=1, throughput was lowest (~6.8k tps). With cache=60% and batch=8 we saw 24k tps and p50 latency 110ms, p95 290ms. With batch=16 throughput rose to 30k but p95 hit 380ms which breaches your 300ms target. So there's a sweet spot at batch 8 with modest batch latency cap.
05:35 Speaker 2 (Lydia): That seems actionable. How reproducible are these numbers with our traffic?
05:40 Speaker 3 (Samir): That's why we want your trace. We can replay with the same arrival patterns and give you expected tokens/sec/$ and latency distributions. Also note our KV cache effectiveness depends on prompt normalization — small variations in whitespace or user tokens reduce hits.
06:00 Speaker 5 (Anika): We have product constraints: 90% of conversations are < 80 tokens. So most responses are short; that biases toward more importance on batching efficiency rather than per-request latency.
06:12 Speaker 3 (Samir): Right, in that case batching with a low max-wait and prefix caching yields the best unit economics. Quantization also helps since your model size is medium.
06:20 Speaker 4 (Tom): On the Dedicated pricing — curious about reserved vs on-demand committed pricing. If we commit for 6 months can we get a lower per-hour and how does that shift tokens/$?
06:31 Speaker 1 (Maya): Yes reserved contracts reduce the effective infra hourly cost which raises tokens/$ significantly. We included a reserved example in the sheet — about 20-25% uplift in tokens/$ when you commit to a monthly reserved pool vs on-demand. Exact numbers depend on region and instance type.
06:46 Speaker 3 (Samir): Also consider autoscaling and burst policies. If you run a smaller reserved pool with burst to shared capacity you get cost savings while still handling spikes. But there's complexity around cold starts and warmup of KV cache.
07:04 Speaker 2 (Lydia): Any guidance on warmup? If we rely on cache, what's the warm window, and will early traffic suffer?
07:11 Speaker 3 (Samir): Warmup depends on traffic pattern; for FAQ-style repeated prompts it can be minutes; for more diverse queries it may not reach high hit-rate quickly. We recommend a hybrid: pre-warm top N prefixes (we can ingest top 200 of your queries) and let runtime learn the rest. That gives immediate cost benefits.
07:30 Speaker 5 (Anika): Can Redwood ingest our historical top queries automatically or do we have to transform them?
07:35 Speaker 3 (Samir): You can drop a CSV of normalized prompts, we'll run them through a small offline job to compute KV entries and pre-populate the cache in the Dedicated pool. Need permissions to read the file; all data is kept under your account and encrypted.
07:49 Speaker 4 (Tom): Back to tokens/sec/$ — could you walk through the math in the sheet? How do you convert GPU-hours to token cost?
07:57 Speaker 3 (Samir): Sure. We take sustained tokens/sec observed on the benchmark, multiply by seconds in month to get monthly tokens capacity, then divide total infra cost (reserved + infra overhead + licensing) by that token volume. We also include amortized control-plane and storage costs. The sheet shows both per-100k-token and per-token numbers for clarity.
08:22 Speaker 2 (Lydia): And the cache savings are modeled as avoided compute -- is there any storage cost for KV cache that materially affects unit economics?
08:31 Speaker 3 (Samir): KV storage is tiny relative to GPU cost for typical LLMs; only when you keep enormous prefix histories (multi-GB per customer) does it matter. For your FAQ use-case it's negligible.
08:43 Speaker 1 (Maya): Quick pause for any blockers on the security side — Maya to send SOC2 summary?
08:50 Speaker 5 (Anika): We also need SAML/SSO and IP allowlist for Dedicated.
08:55 Speaker 1 (Maya): Yes we support SAML SSO and IP allowlist. I'll attach the security questionnaire answers after the call.
09:02 Speaker 4 (Tom): On the benchmarking side, what's the instrumentation you provide so we can validate tokens accounting and latency in our own monitoring?
09:10 Speaker 3 (Samir): We provide per-token latency histograms, per-request detailed logs (sampled), and cost breakdowns per route. You can export these as CSV or we can push metrics into your Datadog.
09:22 Speaker 2 (Lydia): Good. One concern — we sometimes do long generation in a few flows (500+ tokens). Does batching still help for mixes of long and short?
09:31 Speaker 3 (Samir): Longer responses increase per-request compute time and reduce batching headroom because they hold the GPU. But prefix caching still helps because initial prefix compute is amortized. For mixed workloads a mixture of smaller pools for low-latency short replies and larger dedicated for long-run heavy generation is an option. We can simulate hybrid routing.
09:52 Speaker 1 (Maya): Let's get concrete on the next benchmark: we will run three steady-state tests — conservative (cache 40%, batch 8), baseline (cache 60%, batch 8), aggressive (cache 80%, batch 16) — measure tokens/sec, p50, p95, and cost per 100k tokens. Samir will run and post results.
10:15 Speaker 3 (Samir): I'll also include a sensitivity table that maps cache hit from 30% to 90% to tokens/$ and latency.
10:22 Speaker 5 (Anika): For the cost spreadsheet please show both hosted and dedicated columns so stakeholders can see delta.
10:28 Speaker 1 (Maya): Will do.
10:32 Speaker 2 (Lydia): One nit on measurements — please include tokenization differences (some tokens map differently across tokenizers). We use tiktoken v3 in-house.
10:40 Speaker 3 (Samir): Noted — I'll tokenize with tiktoken v3 to match.
10:44 Speaker 4 (Tom): Any enterprise legal/procurement blockers? We got initial SOW but haven't signed procurement.
10:50 Speaker 1 (Maya): Procurement path usually follows the reserved pool commitment. We'll include the standard SOW and licensing terms. I'll coordinate with you, Tom.
10:58 Speaker 5 (Anika): Timeline: we want pilot conclusion and decision by end of July. Is that feasible?
11:04 Speaker 1 (Maya): Yes, if we run the dedicated benchmarks this week and have your trace we'll aim to deliver final numbers in 7-10 days.
11:10 Speaker 3 (Samir): Quick note on cost optimizations we didn't touch — model distillation and smaller model family for certain routes can improve tokens/$ massively. Worth exploring in a follow-up.
11:20 Speaker 2 (Lydia): Agreed, but first let's get baseline numbers.
11:24 Speaker 1 (Maya): Ok last section — recap and next steps.
11:28 Speaker 1 (Maya): Recap: Samir to run three benchmarks and update spreadsheet; Lydia to share 24h trace; Maya to send security docs and updated pricing; schedule Dedicated benchmark times.
11:40 Speaker 5 (Anika): Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
11:45 Speaker 1 (Maya): Thanks — we'll follow up in email, and I'll add action items to the CRM.
11:50 Speaker 2 (Lydia): Bye.
